paragraphs: This paper examines how a sensory system could represent positions more precisely than the spacing between its receptors. Its starting point is a model in which receptors respond broadly but are arranged in an orderly sensory map. The central idea is that fine resolution can emerge from their combined responses, even when individual receptors have broad sensitivity.

The authors extend that model to polynomial weighting schemes: rules that combine receptor responses using weights described by polynomials. They prove that the resulting response is a polynomial of the same order. This establishes a predictable relationship between the mathematical form of the weighting and the form of the system's response.

They also show that Hermitian polynomials are eigenfunctions, meaning that the system preserves their form while potentially changing their scale. These results support a proposed biologically plausible mechanism for representing stimuli at resolutions finer than receptor separation. The contribution is a mathematical account of how an organized population of broadly tuned receptors could support hyperacuity.
neurips-1988-a-model-for-resolution-enha.tldr: An extended sensory-map model explains how combining broadly tuned receptors could yield resolution finer than receptor spacing.

paragraphs: The paper describes a programmable analog machine for running neural networks and simulating their behavior. Its intended applications include visual and acoustic pattern analysis, robotics, and development of specialized networks. The design aims to support computations that interact with the world in real time, using interconnected modules containing neurons, adjustable synapses, and switches.

Network computation takes place in analog circuitry, while digital controls set the connection arrangement, synaptic gains, time constants, and neuron parameters. This separates the physical execution of a network from its configuration. The machine is scalable, but each neuron has a limited number of inputs: it can connect to any other neuron without being connected to all of them simultaneously.

For learning and determining synaptic gains, neuron outputs are multiplexed, converted into digital values, and stored in memory. The design therefore combines analog network operation with digital access to its activity. The authors anticipate a substantial speed advantage over contemporary digital computers; the abstract presents that advantage as an expectation of the proposed architecture.
neurips-1988-a-programmable-analog-neura.tldr: A modular neural computer combines analog computation with digital configuration and access to neuron outputs for learning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates learning a preprocessing step for detecting signals in impulsive, strongly non-Gaussian noise. Under these conditions, minimum-error receivers require a nonlinear transformation before matched filtering. The authors ask whether a neural network can learn the necessary clipping behavior, which limits the influence of unusually large sample values before the detector processes them.

They train a multilayer perceptron with one input, one output, and two hidden layers containing 20 and 5 nodes. Using backpropagation and examples of noiseless and corrupted waveform samples, the network learns a clipping nonlinearity in fewer than 5,000 presentations. Its role is a sample transformation at the detector's front end, while the subsequent matched filter remains linear.

When trained at a relatively high signal-to-noise ratio, the network substantially reduces detection errors when paired with that filter. Its learned transformation resembles the clipping functions used in receivers designed for impulsive noise and provides similar improvements. The result shows that training can recover a useful receiver component whose shape would otherwise be specified through receiver design.
neurips-1988-adaptive-neural-net-preproc.tldr: A small neural network learns a clipping function that substantially improves matched-filter detection in impulsive noise.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a hardware requirement for adaptive neural networks: stored weights must be easy to change during learning. MOS charge storage already offered a way to represent weights in integrated circuits, but storage alone did not provide an on-chip learning mechanism. The authors develop and test a circuit that supports the updates themselves.

The circuit connects two capacitors through a structure resembling a charge-coupled device. It allows weight changes of variable size and provides a weight-decay operation. These capabilities address the need for fine adjustments during iterative learning, when weights may repeatedly increase and decrease. The supplied discussion explains that coarse weight resolution can undermine the search for better settings near existing ones.

One fabricated CMOS implementation achieves more than 10 bits of dynamic range. A smaller-process chip based on the same cell contains 1,104 weights and supports peak learning rates of at least two billion weight changes per second. These results make the contribution concrete: a weight-storage cell designed to participate directly in rapid, repeated adaptation.
neurips-1988-adaptive-neural-networks-us.tldr: A fabricated charge-storage circuit supports fine, variable-sized weight updates and decay for learning directly in neural hardware.

paragraphs: ALVINN is a three-layer neural network designed to steer a vehicle along a road. It takes images from a camera and a laser range finder and produces a direction of travel. The task connects sensory input directly to a driving decision: which direction will keep the vehicle following the road.

The network is trained with backpropagation using simulated road images. Successful tests on Carnegie Mellon's autonomous navigation test vehicle show that this training can support road following in the physical world under certain field conditions. The stated result therefore connects learning from simulation with operation on real roads, while retaining the abstract's qualification about the conditions of those tests.

The authors also find that the network develops markedly different internal representations under different training conditions. This matters because the same general architecture can organize its processing differently depending on what it encounters during learning. They interpret that flexibility as suggesting an adaptive navigation system that could tailor its processing to prevailing conditions, rather than reporting that broader capability as already established.
neurips-1988-alvinn-an-autonomous-land-v.tldr: ALVINN learns road following from simulated images and successfully guides a real vehicle under certain field conditions.

paragraphs: TIN2 learns how a sequential system changes state by observing its behavior. A transition function describes how the system's current state and incoming information determine what happens next. Learning such a function requires a useful representation of state as well as a way to connect states through transitions.

The architecture divides these responsibilities between two subnets. TIN-2 constructs state representations from behavioral examples, and its dynamics receive particular attention in the paper. TIN-I learns transition functions from noisy state representations and environmental data. During operation, TIN-I generates sequences of transitions as the input changes. Both subnets use dynamics based on Adaptive Resonance Theory.

The reported experiment concerns a system that recognizes strings containing an even number of ones. This provides a concrete sequential task in which recognition depends on the accumulated history of the input. The paper reports that TIN2 learns this system's behavior, illustrating how learned state representations and learned transition rules can work together within one adaptive network.
neurips-1988-an-adaptive-network-that-le.tldr: TIN2 combines learned state representations with learned transition rules to reproduce a sequential system's behavior.

paragraphs: The paper describes an electronic light receptor designed to detect small changes in illumination. It extends an earlier circuit whose output voltage varies logarithmically with light intensity. The key addition sends a filtered version of the output back to the input, making feedback central to the circuit's sensitivity to changes.

The feedback loop includes a hysteretic element, whose behavior depends on its prior state. Together with two amplification stages, this produces responses resembling the gain control and timing behavior of retinal cells, particularly bipolar cells. The circuit therefore provides a physical implementation of a proposed sensory principle: feedback can help a receptor respond to changes around its illumination level.

The authors compare intensity-increment detection thresholds in the circuit and a human observer. Both follow Weber's law, meaning that detectable increments scale with the background intensity, and their temporal contrast sensitivities are nearly identical. The supplied circuit analysis also reports logarithmic operation under a subthreshold assumption valid across about four orders of magnitude, connecting the observed behavior to the electronics.
neurips-1988-an-electronic-photoreceptor.tldr: Filtered feedback makes an electronic photoreceptor sensitive to small light changes, with detection behavior closely resembling human vision.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to execute probabilistic rule systems in parallel using connectionist architectures. Probabilistic rules express relationships with uncertainty, so the problem involves more than applying rules as absolute statements. The authors use information-theoretic models as the basis for giving these rules a quantitative meaning and building networks that perform inference with them.

The presentation begins with a non-neural learning algorithm and a theory of quantitative rule modeling. It then examines two particular models before turning to the inference architecture. This sequence connects the way rules are learned and interpreted with the way a network executes them, making the underlying rule semantics part of the architectural design.

A worked example follows the entire route from a database to rules and then to an inference network. The authors compare the resulting network's performance with theoretical limits for specific problems. That comparison frames the network as an implementation of a defined probabilistic reasoning procedure, allowing its behavior to be assessed against the theory that motivated it.
neurips-1988-an-information-theoretic-ap.tldr: The paper connects information-theoretic rule learning with parallel inference networks and evaluates them against problem-specific theoretical limits.

paragraphs: This paper trains a neural network to decide whether a handwritten signature is genuine or forged. Its input is a binary image of the signature, and its output comes from a single decision unit. A hidden layer sits between the image and the output, with connection weights adjusted through backpropagation.

The signatures are captured with an electronic digitizing camera and entered into a C program. Before reaching the network, the binary images are normalized and centered. This preprocessing gives the learning system a more consistent presentation of each signature. The study then examines how performance changes with the training set and the structure of the network.

The best reported results are approximately 2% rejection of genuine signatures and 2–4% acceptance of false signatures. These describe two distinct errors: refusing an authentic signature and accepting an impostor's signature. Reporting both makes the verification outcome more informative than a single combined score. The results demonstrate that this image-based feedforward network can learn a useful distinction between genuine and forged examples.
neurips-1988-backpropagation-and-its-app.tldr: A backpropagation network verifies signature images, with best reported errors near 2% genuine rejection and 2–4% false acceptance.

paragraphs: The paper proposes expanding what a neural network changes during supervised learning. In the setup it critiques, connection weights adapt while each neuron's nonlinear response remains fixed. The authors allow parameters of the neurons themselves to participate in learning, giving the training process another way to represent the relationships in its examples.

Their specific example is the temperature parameter of a sigmoid response function. This parameter controls the shape of the neuron's response to its input. Each neuron has its own local temperature, which is updated alongside the synaptic weights. Learning therefore adjusts both how strongly neurons influence one another and how individual neurons respond to those influences.

The algorithm is applied to logic tasks including XOR and parity. The authors report a significant reduction in the number of training cycles and describe a corresponding reduction in supervised-learning computation time. The finding supports the idea that trainable response parameters can make learning more efficient on these tasks, rather than treating all adaptation as a change in connection strengths.
neurips-1988-does-the-neuron-learn-like-.tldr: Learning each neuron's sigmoid temperature alongside connection weights substantially reduces training cycles on XOR and parity tasks.

paragraphs: This paper examines how delayed neuron responses affect the behavior of analog neural networks. The central issue is whether activity settles or continues changing indefinitely. A response delay can alter that outcome: the authors identify sustained oscillation and chaos as behaviors that delays can induce.

For networks with symmetric connections, the paper develops a criterion intended to prevent sustained oscillation. It derives this criterion through local stability analysis, which examines behavior near an equilibrium. This links a property of the network's dynamics to a practical question about its operation: whether delayed responses allow activity to settle rather than keep cycling.

The authors also present an example of chaotic dynamics in a network with nonsymmetric connections. The two contributions address different settings: a stability condition for symmetric delay networks and an example of chaos in a nonsymmetric one. Together, they show why response timing belongs in the analysis of analog networks. Understanding the connections alone is insufficient when delayed activity can change the network's eventual behavior.
neurips-1988-dynamics-of-analog-neural-n.tldr: Response delays can produce oscillation or chaos, motivating a stability criterion for symmetric analog neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper describes synthetic receptors intended for tactile and haptic sensing. Their sensing mechanism is magnetic: the receptors use Hall-effect structures fabricated with standard CMOS technology. The contribution connects a physical sensing element with integrated-circuit fabrication, presenting magnetic-field measurements as a basis for electronic receptors.

A small permanent magnet provides a bias field for the receptors. In this arrangement, they can detect nearby ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic objects. The stated sensing capability is therefore tied to objects with those magnetic properties. The presence-detection function concerns objects in the sensor's vicinity, making proximity part of the proposed receptor's operation.

The receptors can also detect the magnitude and direction of a magnetic field. This gives the design a richer measurement capability than a simple indication that a suitable object is nearby: it can register both field strength and orientation. Together, these capabilities define the paper's proposal for haptic sensing through CMOS magnetic receptors and a small permanent magnet.
neurips-1988-electronic-receptors-for-ta.tldr: CMOS Hall-effect receptors use a small permanent magnet to sense nearby magnetic objects and measure field magnitude and direction.

paragraphs: The paper introduces supervised learning algorithms for approximating piecewise-continuous functions. Inspired by the CMAC model, they combine local representations, hashing, and several levels of resolution. This arrangement represents a function at different scales, allowing the approximation to account for both broader structure and more localized variation.

The authors report learning speeds orders of magnitude faster than typical backpropagation implementations, while often obtaining comparable generalization. The qualification matters: similar performance on new inputs is reported frequently, rather than as an unconditional guarantee. The approach targets situations where an adaptive system must update its behavior quickly enough to be useful during ongoing signal processing.

The algorithms are also described as efficiently capturing complicated nonlinear structure beyond the capabilities of the simpler adaptive systems discussed in the abstract. A prediction task involving a chaotic time series illustrates the method. The broader contribution is a representation strategy that connects rapid supervised updates with nonlinear function approximation, making learning speed a central feature of the design.
neurips-1988-fast-learning-in-multi-reso.tldr: Local, hashed representations at multiple resolutions enable much faster learning than typical backpropagation, often with comparable generalization.

paragraphs: GENESIS is a general-purpose simulation system designed to make neural-network modeling easier. It is graphically oriented and implemented under UNIX and X-windows. Its central design goal is to support models at multiple levels of detail, accommodating different choices about how much neural structure a simulation represents.

The intended scope includes applied neural-network modeling and detailed models grounded in biology. These uses ask different questions of a simulator: an abstract connectionist model emphasizes network computation, while a biologically detailed model represents more of the underlying neural system. GENESIS is designed to provide a simulation environment broad enough for both kinds of work.

The abstract identifies existing models of the mammalian olfactory bulb and cortex, invertebrate central pattern generators, and more abstract connectionist networks. These examples demonstrate the range of modeling already undertaken with the system. The paper's contribution is therefore a shared simulation platform spanning several neural systems and levels of abstraction, with its graphical orientation supporting the overall modeling workflow.
neurips-1988-genesis-a-system-for-simula.tldr: GENESIS provides a graphical simulation environment for neural models ranging from abstract networks to detailed biological systems.

paragraphs: The paper describes automatically developed representations that encode hierarchical data structures in analog vectors of fixed width. The structures being represented can vary in size, while the number of components in their vector representations stays fixed. Their recursive organization allows representations to address data whose parts are themselves structured.

One implication is that certain data structures associated with symbolic artificial intelligence can be expressed in a form suitable for neural-network processing. The author states that simple inferences can then be performed through pattern associations. This links structured information with an operation neural networks handle naturally: learning relationships between distributed patterns.

A second implication concerns the representations' mathematical behavior. The author reports that they become self-similar in the limit, connecting the work to questions about chaos and the representational foundations of intelligence. The contribution thus has both a computational and a conceptual aspect: fixed-width vectors can support some structured reasoning, while their recursive form raises further questions about the geometry and dynamics of representation.
neurips-1988-implications-of-recursive-d.tldr: Recursive distributed representations encode variable-sized hierarchical structures in fixed-width vectors and support simple inference through pattern association.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a learning algorithm for multilayer networks built from binary linear threshold units. Such units produce binary outputs according to whether their weighted inputs cross a threshold. The algorithm makes the network's internal representations the primary objects to determine during training.

This changes the organization of the learning problem. Instead of beginning with a cost function over connection weights, the method seeks a correct set of internal representations. Once those representations have been established, the weights are learned using the Perceptron Learning Rule. The authors describe that rule as local and biologically plausible, giving the representation choices a route to concrete connection strengths.

The algorithm is tested on adjacency, symmetry, parity, and a combined symmetry-parity problem. These tasks provide distinct settings for examining the approach. The main contribution is the separation between deciding what the intermediate units should represent and determining weights that realize those decisions. That separation offers an alternative way to formulate multilayer learning around the internal organization of the solution.
neurips-1988-learning-by-choice-of-inter.tldr: The algorithm learns multilayer threshold networks by choosing internal representations first and then fitting weights with the Perceptron Learning Rule.

paragraphs: The paper models how a visual system can learn a pattern's true direction of motion from incomplete local measurements. A detector viewing a moving edge can register the motion component perpendicular to that edge, leaving the full direction ambiguous. This is the aperture problem: individual edge measurements do not directly specify the motion of the whole pattern.

The authors use a multilayer feedforward network trained with a Hebb rule. Input patterns contain randomly oriented contours moving in a particular direction. The input units are assigned direction and speed sensitivities resembling those of neurons projecting from visual area V1 to MT, so the network begins with biologically motivated component-motion signals.

After exposure to many patterns, training continues until most weights saturate. A proportion of second-layer units acquire responses that solve the aperture problem and resemble pattern-direction-selective neurons in MT. The result shows that learning from varied moving contours can produce a more complete motion representation from component-sensitive inputs, with the reported capability emerging in some units.
neurips-1988-learning-the-solution-to-th.tldr: Hebbian learning produces units that recover pattern motion from locally ambiguous edge-motion signals.

paragraphs: Classifier systems use genetic algorithms as their learning mechanism and differ substantially from conventional neural networks in their internal organization and representations. This paper asks whether those differences imply fundamentally different computational formalisms. Its answer is developed through a transformation that connects the behavior of the two kinds of system.

The paper describes how to map classifier systems into neural networks that preserve their behavior. This supplies one direction of an equivalence argument; a companion paper supplies the other direction. The result is therefore a constructive correspondence: it explains how a system expressed in one formalism can be represented through the other.

The transformation requires several changes to commonly used neural-network paradigms, and the authors discuss whether those changes are appropriate. That qualification defines the scope of the equivalence: the mapping depends on the specified alterations. The paper also considers practical implications and possible extensions, showing how apparently different learning-system descriptions can be related through their behavior despite substantial differences in representation and learning mechanisms.
neurips-1988-mapping-classifier-systems-.tldr: A constructive mapping converts classifier systems into behaviorally equivalent neural networks with specified changes to conventional network designs.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes winner-take-all selection from finding one largest value to identifying the K largest values among N real numbers. It implements that operation using a continuous Hopfield network. Each node starts with one input value, and the network's evolving state determines which positions belong to the selected group.

The nodes inhibit one another, while a shared external input depends on the requested number of winners and the network size. When the sigmoid gain is sufficiently large, the network converges to positive states at the positions of the K largest initial values and negative states elsewhere. The final signs therefore encode membership in the selected set.

The authors rigorously analyze equilibrium states, stable equilibria, and the network's dynamics. This analysis connects the desired selection operation to the behavior of the continuous system implementing it. The gain condition is part of the stated result: selection emerges under a sufficiently sharp sigmoid response. The contribution is a mathematically examined network mechanism for selecting multiple winners.
neurips-1988-on-the-k-winners-take-all-n.tldr: A continuous Hopfield network identifies the K largest inputs through stable positive and negative states when sigmoid gain is sufficiently high.

paragraphs: Weakly electric fish explore by generating electric pulses and sensing how nearby objects disturb the resulting fields. Their sensory input is a sequence of electric images whose spatial and temporal properties depend on the fish's position and discharge timing. Understanding object discrimination therefore requires understanding how the animal's own behavior changes the signals it receives.

The authors develop a finite-element simulation of the fish's self-generated electric field. Its purpose is to reconstruct the electrosensory consequences of body position and the timing of electric-organ discharges. By representing the field computationally, the system provides a way to investigate the relationship between exploratory behavior and the resulting sensory images.

The paper presents the simulation system alongside preliminary field measurements used to tune it. These measurements connect the computational reconstruction to the physical fields being modeled. The contribution is a tool for studying how movement and pulse timing may aid object discrimination, with the reported work centered on constructing and calibrating that tool.
neurips-1988-simulation-and-measurement-.tldr: A finite-element electric-field simulator, tuned with preliminary measurements, supports study of how fish movement and pulse timing shape sensory input.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical account of how organized sensory maps can emerge through changes in neural connections. Its main example is the formation of ocular dominance columns, where inputs associated with the two eyes become spatially organized in primary visual cortex. The authors treat this organization as a process arising from interacting physiological mechanisms.

Three hypotheses drive the model: synapses compete for trophic factors, their growth or retraction depends on coincident presynaptic activity and postsynaptic depolarization, and lateral connections exist before modification begins. Coupled equations describe electrical activity and connection density. Because electrical activity changes much faster than synapses grow or retract, the analysis uses an approximation that separates those time scales.

Monte Carlo simulations examine the segregation of inputs from the two sides. The authors report that a phase-transition interpretation explains almost all the physiological findings they consider for cats and monkeys raised under normal or abnormal visual conditions. The result connects local rules for synaptic change with large-scale cortical patterns and their dependence on visual experience.
neurips-1988-theory-of-self-organization.tldr: A physiologically motivated model explains ocular dominance pattern formation through synaptic competition, activity-dependent change, and phase-transition behavior.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a very small neural network can be trained to match every example in a supplied training set. The network has two layers, three nodes, and an arbitrary number of inputs. Each node computes a linear threshold function, producing its output by comparing a weighted input sum with a threshold.

The authors prove that deciding whether suitable weights and thresholds exist is NP-complete. This is a statement about the computational difficulty of the exact consistency problem, even for this compact architecture. They extend the result to other simple networks, showing that small size or regular structure alone does not remove the difficulty of finding a perfect fit.

The result motivates attention to the choice of network and input encoding for a particular task. A simple-looking architecture can still lead to a difficult training problem, so architecture alone is an unreliable guide to tractability. The proof concerns threshold units; extending it to nonlinear response functions such as sigmoids is explicitly left open.
neurips-1988-training-a-3-node-neural-ne.tldr: Finding an exact fit is NP-complete even for a three-node threshold network, so architectural simplicity does not guarantee easy training.

paragraphs: The paper examines a difficulty in implementing neural networks as integrated circuits: individual nodes may require too many connections. One response is to replace highly connected feedforward networks with functionally equivalent networks using fewer inputs per node and additional layers. That substitution changes the problem of choosing and learning connection weights.

The authors identify two obstacles. There is no direct mapping of weights from a fully connected network to its limited-interconnect counterpart. In addition, nonlinear processing at lower levels can prevent internal representations from combining widely separated spatial features. Gradient-descent training is also hindered because error magnitudes dissipate, weakening the information available for reducing output error.

The proposed remedy is a careful use of linear summations, or collection units. These units provide a way to gather information while addressing the difficulties attributed to early nonlinear transformations. The paper's central point is that preserving a network's possible input-output function does not automatically preserve straightforward training: connection constraints, internal representations, and error propagation must be considered together.
neurips-1988-training-a-limited-intercon.tldr: Linear collection units are proposed to ease representation and training problems in neural hardware with limited connections.

paragraphs: This paper addresses slow training in multilayer perceptrons. The authors describe backpropagation as requiring many iterations on large or complex problems, with speech recognition motivating the concern. Their approach changes the mathematical framing of training so that a different estimation method can be applied.

They formulate training as identification of a nonlinear dynamic system. In this view, learning means determining system parameters from the available examples. The Extended Kalman Algorithm then provides a procedure for estimating those parameters. The paper describes the method and compares it with backpropagation on two-dimensional examples, making the comparison concrete at that scale.

The authors report that the Kalman approach usually converges in a few iterations, while also emphasizing its computational complexity. The relevant tradeoff is therefore between the number of iterations and the work required by the algorithm. The result suggests that a more elaborate update procedure can substantially reduce iteration counts, without making iteration count alone a complete measure of training cost.
neurips-1988-training-multilayer-percept.tldr: Treating perceptron training as nonlinear system identification enables Extended Kalman updates that usually converge in few, computationally complex iterations.

paragraphs: The paper reports preliminary work on speaker-independent speech recognition using multilayer networks and phonetic features. Its approach combines neural-network knowledge with speech-recognition expertise. A central design choice is how the incoming sound is represented before recognition, with different processing proposed for different kinds of speech.

For transient sounds, the system uses event-driven property extractors with variable resolution in time and frequency. These sounds are handled through features organized around acoustic events, with the analysis resolution allowed to vary. For sonorant speech, the authors instead prefer a model of the human auditory system as the front end over an FFT-based representation.

The contribution is a recognition-system design that makes speech-specific processing part of the neural approach. Transient and sonorant sounds receive different front ends because the method explicitly distinguishes their acoustic character. The reported findings are preliminary, so the stated significance lies in this combination of domain-informed feature extraction and multilayer networks for the speaker-independent recognition task.
neurips-1988-use-of-multi-layered-networ.tldr: The paper combines multilayer networks with speech-specific front ends for preliminary speaker-independent recognition.
